title: Say it, then stand firm
hook: say, I believe in Allah, and then be upright (Nawawi 21, Sufyan ibn Abdullah)
tomorrow: a man swears he'll do the basics and not one thing more. and then?

segments.voice: A week of the forty, back in your hands. Good, or silent. Don't be angry. Even the blade. The good erases it. He will protect you. And yesterday: shame guards.
screen: `GOOD, OR SILENT · DON'T BE ANGRY · EVEN THE BLADE` → `THE GOOD ERASES IT · HE WILL PROTECT YOU · SHAME GUARDS`

segments.voice: A man wants one sentence he'll never need to ask about again. Some people want the full manual; others want one line to tape to the fridge. Neither is wrong. In al-Nawawi's twenty-first hadith, Sufyan ibn Abdullah asks for the fridge kind: tell me something about Islam I won't need to ask anyone else about. Sufyan isn't asking for a lecture. He wants a sentence he can carry out the door, the kind you could say in a single breath. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gives him one, in two moves.
screen: `THE MANUAL, OR THE FRIDGE?` → `ONE SENTENCE.` → `TWO MOVES.`

segments.voice: From Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase: say, I believe in Allah, and then be upright. The Arabic for that last part is istaqim: stand straight, stay on course, don't drift. Two moves. First you say it. Then you stand, and standing takes the rest of your life. The Qur'an praises those who say, our Lord is Allah, and then stay upright on it, and says the angels come down to them with comfort. Saying is a day; standing is every day after. And notice what Sufyan asked for: something he'd never need to ask anyone else about. The answer isn't a secret fact. It's a direction. Once you have it, the question changes from what do I believe to am I still standing in it today. Now look back, because this was a week of standing. The tongue held at good or silent. The heat lowered before it spoke. The blade sharpened when nobody would check. The bad deed followed by a good one. Allah kept in mind while the pages felt unfinished. And shame left on guard. Six small ways of staying upright. None of them dramatic. All of them standing. Next week, more of the forty. Believe, then stand.
screen: `SAY: I BELIEVE IN ALLAH.` · `ISTAQIM: STAND STRAIGHT.` · `SAYING IS A DAY. STANDING IS AFTER.` · `A WEEK OF STANDING.` · then, large: `BELIEVE, THEN STAND.`

segments.voice: Choose one practice from this week, the one you most want to still be doing next Friday. Name the moment it's most likely to slip. Then make the plan in one short sentence, when this happens, I'll do that, small enough to keep on your worst day, and hold it for the sit.
Say it: the hadith's first move, I believe in Allah. Then comes istaqim, the standing that takes longer, and that you keep on doing.
To keep: believe, then stand, because the sentence is short and the standing is long. A week of the forty, done.

screen: `DAY 1449 COUNTS.` → `THE FORTY · 21 OF 42.` → `TOMORROW: A MAN SWEARS HE'LL DO THE BASICS AND NOT ONE THING MORE. AND THEN?`

howItsDone: Muslims often cite this hadith for steadiness over bursts; teachers pair it with Qur'an 41:30 and encourage small deeds kept up rather than big ones dropped.
